master_output.idea:
**Mocking:** myself, a researcher

Let me start from what I actually care about. I want the final saved prediction file to be correct — but what makes a prediction correct? It's the probability that the model outputs, not the raw argmax. So the naive way of just saving predictions as labels is a lossy truncation. That's my observation: saving argmax is throwing away information I actually need. That's not a bug — it's the natural consequence of a pipeline that's trained and evaluated on labels. And the reason it's hard to see is that nobody has ever asked whether the model's per-class probabilities are being saved. Nobody has ever asked the question that would break the pipeline.

So I'm forced to ask the uncomfortable question: what if I never actually evaluate the model on the test set? If I save the argmax labels, I can't even check how good they are — I don't have the ground truth. That means I have two separate evaluation tasks: one on the training set, and one on the test set. The one on the training set is cheap and tells me whether the model is overfitting; the one on the test set is expensive and tells me whether it's generalizing. But if I never do the expensive one, I'm flying blind — and I'm saving a file whose quality I cannot confirm.

Why does this cut against the instinct? Because the instinct is: train, validate, save labels, done. The obvious cost is that doing a second evaluation costs time and memory — more tokens, more GPU time, more storage. But the honest cost is that I can't know if the file is wrong. So the trade is measured not in lines of code but in whether the file is correct.

Now the crux of the leap. The thing that lets me keep the expensive evaluation and still keep the file cheap is that I can recompute probabilities on the fly. The model already has a predict_proba method — and I can run that on the test set's tokenized inputs, then save the raw probabilities (the class distribution, not a label), and then derive the label from it. That means I only run the full model once on the test set. The cost is amortized over the saved file — I pay for the prediction once, and get the probabilities forever. I save a file with richer information, and I get the quality guarantee that the file is correct.

How do I keep myself honest, and what's the catch? I need to make the saved file reproducible: the same seed, the same tokenizer, the same model weights. If I change anything, I have to recompute it, and the guarantee only holds for that exact configuration. So the decision rule is: if I ever change the pipeline, I must recompute the probabilities and re-derive the labels — the saved file is only valid for that one run. And I must verify the saved file against the test set labels (which I can now do, since I re-ran the expensive evaluation) before trusting it. That's the discipline the idea needs, or it's just a pretty story.

**Core idea:** Save raw per-class probabilities instead of argmax labels, so the model's quality on the test set is verifiable, and re-derive the label at prediction time to keep the saved file cheap and reproducible.

**Non-trivial crux:** The guarantee only holds if you re-run the expensive evaluation and recompute probabilities under the same exact pipeline; otherwise the saved file's correctness is unverifiable and the label derivation is an extra step you must re-run after every pipeline change.
